The SEA host the SF as favorites of 3.5, with the total set at 48.5 — a market that implies a SEA 26–22 scoreline. Running the game forward from that baseline, we expect a contest that spends roughly 33% of its snaps with SEA in front, 42% within one score, and 25% with SEA chasing. That distribution is the engine of everything below: game state is what turns a team's tendencies into a specific player's workload, so before we get to individuals it's worth being explicit about how this game is likely to be played.

A modest edge to SEA. They should lead more often than not, tilting them slightly toward the run late, while SF leans a touch more pass-heavy to stay in it — but the effect is gentle; this isn't a script that dramatically reshapes anyone's usage.

The Key Matchups

Tough sledding for Christian McCaffrey — SEA are stingy against the run (106 yds/game, well below the ~120 norm); lean under on his rushing line.

George Kittle has room to work — SEA allow 42 yds/game to TE1s (vs ~35), a receiving-yards and target angle.

Jaxon Smith-Njigba faces a tough cover — SF hold WR1s to just 51 yds/game (vs ~58); a rec-yards under lean.

Mike Evans faces a tough cover — SEA hold WR1s to just 48 yds/game (vs ~58); a rec-yards under lean.

Touchdown Board

AJ Barner is a live anytime-TD dart — SF are leaky to tight ends in the end zone (0.31 TE TDs/game vs ~0.24).

Game Script, Pace & Environment

A modest lean to SEA — they should lead more often than not, nudging them toward the run late and giving Jadarian Price a gentle game-script tailwind.

SEA — a balanced offense

SEA are a balanced offense — their run/pass split by game state tracks the league closely (43% pass when leading vs 44% average), so their players' usage is driven more by role than by any strong situational lean.

Jadarian Price (12 carries, 52 yards projected) gets a mild game-script tailwind as a favorite, though SEA's willingness to keep throwing when ahead caps how much the lead converts into extra carries.

Jaxon Smith-Njigba projects for 9 targets and 82 yards, in line with his established role in a script that neither inflates nor suppresses the pass.

Underneath, AJ Barner (TE, 3 targets, 26 yards) is the dependable secondary read — and note the red zone stays TE-friendly regardless of score, so his touchdown equity holds up even if the game script shifts.

SF — a run-heavy offense

SF are one of the league's more run-committed offenses: on early downs while leading, they pass just 40% of the time, against a league average of 44% — a genuine clock-bleeding identity, not noise (it holds after shrinking their sample toward the league).

Game script works against the run here — SF project to trail and throw, which squeezes Christian McCaffrey's rushing projection (16 carries, 73 yards) but raises his value as a receiver; trailing teams check the ball down, and his target share ticks up as the game gets away from them.

Mike Evans is the one to target from a volume standpoint: as underdogs throwing to keep pace, SF funnel work to their top receiver — 7 targets for 60 yards projected, with genuine upside if they fall behind early and the game turns one-dimensional.

Underneath, George Kittle (TE, 6 targets, 63 yards) is the dependable secondary read — and note the red zone stays TE-friendly regardless of score, so his touchdown equity holds up even if the game script shifts.

What to watch

The single biggest swing factor is availability — use the injury tool in the sidebar to mark anyone out; a starter's absence doesn't just remove his line, it redistributes his targets and carries to specific teammates, and the report and projections rebuild around it. Beyond that: if this game breaks toward the projected 4-point margin, the garbage-time backups (the ◆-flagged rows below) are where soft lines and real edge tend to appear — those depth players get fed in blowouts, and the market is slowest to price them.

This preview and the projections below regenerate through the week as injuries, weather and line moves update the inputs.
